sentences.text: It has been argued by learned counsel for the appellants that the respondent No. 2 has lodged first information report of this case making false and baseless allegations.

The alleged incident has been shown of 12.09.2021 but the first information report has been lodged after about 6 months on 28.03.2022 and no satisfactory explanation for delay in the FIR has been shown.

Learned counsel submitted that in fact, on 12.09.2021 the family members of respondent No. 2 have assaulted the appellant party and in that incident appellant Nos. 1 to 4 have sustained injuries and in that connection, a first information report was lodged against the family members of the respondent No.2 on the same day i.e. 12.09.2021 and after investigation charge-sheet was submitted in that case.
The first information report of the instant case has been lodged as a counterblast of the said case, by securing false medical examination report.
In the medical examination report, merely simple injuries have been shown.

It is also submitted that even according to the prosecution version,
alleged incident has been shown inside the house of the complainant/respondent No. 2 and thus, no offence under Section 3(2)(Va) of SC/ST Act is made out.

Referring to the facts of the matter, it was submitted that the impugned proceedings are abuse of process of Court and have been initiated as a counterblast of the case lodged earlier from the side of the appellants.

5. Learned A.G.A. and learned counsel for the respondent No. 2 have opposed the appeal and argued that all the appellants are named in the first information report and that in the said incident two persons, namely, Rajesh Sagar and Kamal Sagar, sustained injuries.
The injured persons and other witnesses have supported prosecution version during investigation.
After investigation, police have already submitted charge-sheet against the appellants.

Referring to the facts of the matter, it was submitted that in view of allegations made in the first information report and material collected during investigation, it cannot be said that no case is made out against the appellants.
6. I have considered the rival submissions and perused the record.

7. It is well settled that at the stage of cognizance and at the stage of issuing process to the accused,
the Magistrate has to be satisfied that there is sufficient ground for proceeding.
The court has to consider whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding and not whether there is sufficient ground for conviction.

At the stage of issuing the process to the accused, the Magistrate is not required to record reasons, particularly when the cognizance is being taken on the basis of report filed by the police after investigation, under section 173(2) Cr.P.C. In S.K. Sinha, Chief Enforcement Officer Vs. Videocon International Limited and Ors. MANU/SC/7011/2008 : (2008) 2 SCC 492

entities.text: S.K. Sinha, Chief Enforcement Officer Vs. Videocon International Limited and Ors. MANU/SC/7011/2008 : (2008) 2 SCC 492
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , it was held that taking cognizance has no esoteric or mystic significance in criminal law and it connotes that a judicial notice is taken of an offence, after application of mind.
Taking of cognizance is thus a condition precedent for holding a valid trial.

In M/s. India Carat Pvt. Ltd. Vs. State of Karnataka MANU/SC/0349/1989: 1989(26) ACC 280 (SC), the Supreme Court has observed that Magistrate can take into account statements of witnesses examined by Police during investigation,
take cognizance of offence complained of, order to issue a process to accused.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 8. In Mehmood Ul Rehman v. Khazir Mohammad Tunda and others (2015) 12 SCC 420, it was held as under:-

sentences.text: Under Section 190(1)(b) Cr.P.C, the Magistrate has the advantage of a police report and under Section 190(1)(c) Cr.P.C., he has the information or knowledge of commission of an offence.
But under Section 190(1)(a) Cr.P.C., he has only a complaint before him.
The Code hence specifies that "a complaint of facts which constitute such offence".
Therefore, if the complaint, on the face of it, does not disclose the commission of any offence, the Magistrate shall not take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) Cr.P.C.
The complaint is simply to be rejected."

9. Thus, in so far as taking cognizance based on the police report is concerned, the Magistrate/ court has the advantage of the charge sheet, statement of witnesses and other evidence collected by the police during the investigation.
For issuance of process against the accused, only it has to be seen whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
At the stage of issuance of process, the Court is not required to weigh the evidentiary value of the materials on record.
The Court must apply its mind to the allegations in the charge sheet and the evidence produced and satisfy itself that there is sufficient ground to proceed against the accused.
The Court is not to examine the merits and demerits of the case and not to determine the adequacy of the evidence for holding the accused guilty.
The Court is also not required to embark upon the possible defenses.
Likewise, 'possible defences' need not be taken into consideration at the time of issuing process unless there is an ex- facie defence such as a legal bar or if in law the accused is not liable.

In this connection a reference may also be made to Nupur Talwar v. Central Bureau of Investigation and another (2012)11 SCC465.
10.

entities.text: Nupur Talwar v. Central Bureau of Investigation and another (2012)11 SCC465
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the instant matter, perusal of record shows that the respondent No.2 has lodged first information report of this case against the appellants alleging that on 12.09.2021 at about 12:30 P.M., accused-appellants, armed with lathi, sticks and rods, came at the door of the house of respondent/informant and pressurized him to remove the tree, lying outside his house, and they abused the respondent/informant by using caste indicative words and trespassed into his house and assaulted respondent/informant and his family members and resultantly, Rajesh Sagar and Kamal Sagar sustained injuries.
The injured witnesses have supported the said prosecution version during investigation.
In injury report of injured Rajesh Sagar, two injuries have been shown and in injury report of Kamal Sagar, five injuries have been shown.
In view of allegations made in the first information report and the material collected during investigation, it cannot be said that no prima facie case is made out against the appellants.

It is correct that there is delay of several months in lodging of the first information report and that earlier the appellant No. 1 has lodged a first information report against the family members of the respondent/informant regarding incident of 12.09.2021, but the proceedings of the case cannot be quashed on that ground.
The effect of delay in FIR is to be considered during trial.
In view of above stated facts, no case for quashing of the impugned proceedings, charge-sheet and summoning order is made out, hence, the prayer sought by the appellants is refused.

11. However, considering the facts of the matter it is directed that in case appellants appear/surrender before the trial court within a period of 3 weeks from today and apply for bail,
their bail application shall be considered and decided expeditiously in accordance with settled law.
